events.notes:
This one is **much closer to the tone we want than some of the batch pages**, but I still think it can be sharper and more interesting. The raw ingredients are good; the page just needs a little less nursery-description language and a little more “what should I notice right now?”

My biggest reaction is that the **corn-cob fruit is absolutely the star**. That is the fact I remember five minutes later. The wide leaflets are useful, the bamboo-like trunk is useful, and the male/female plant fact is useful. But the fruit cluster is the thing that gives this species a personality.

The first At a Glance line is therefore excellent:

> The fruit clusters look strikingly like small ears of corn...

Keep it. It is visual, specific, and immediately gives the visitor something to look for. The underlying morphology is real: the female fruiting structure is short, stiff and densely packed, with black fruit compressed tightly together. ([World Flora Online][1])

The **second At a Glance** is useful but a little flat:

> The leaflets are unusually wide for the genus...

I would make it more visual:

> **Most Chamaedorea palms have narrow leaflets. This one looks almost oversized by comparison, with broad, paddle-like leaflets that can be several inches wide.**

That lets the visitor picture the difference instead of being told it is “unusually wide.”

The **third At a Glance** is accurate enough, but it reads like catalog copy:

> A solitary palm that tops out around twelve to thirteen feet...

I’d loosen it:

> **It stays surprisingly slim even when mature — roughly twelve feet tall on a trunk barely thicker than your wrist.**

The published botanical description gives stems up to about 4 m tall and only 2–3 cm thick. ([World Flora Online][1]) That proportion is much more interesting than the raw dimensions.

events.notes:
Yes — **this is much better.** It feels like a human showing me the palm now, not a nursery catalog describing it. I’d call it close, with a few worthwhile tweaks.

The biggest thing I’d change is this line:

> roughly twelve feet tall on a trunk barely thicker than your wrist.

The published dimensions put the trunk around **an inch or so thick**, which is actually *thinner* than most adult wrists. That makes the fact better! I’d say:

> **It can reach roughly twelve feet tall on a trunk only about an inch thick.**

Or, more conversationally:

> **It can reach roughly twelve feet tall on a trunk not much thicker than your thumb.**

That is weird enough on its own.

I also like the new **wide-leaflet** wording a lot more. One tiny caution:

> noticeably different from the narrow, strap-like leaflets of its relatives.

Not all its relatives have narrow leaflets, so I’d make that:

> noticeably different from the narrow, strap-like leaflets of **many** of its relatives.

That keeps the nice comparison without overclaiming.

The fruit section is now **excellent**:

> The fruits are squeezed close enough that they press into slightly angular shapes.

That detail makes the corn comparison feel earned rather than cute. Keep it.

### Where it comes from

This is clean now. I might shave a little horticultural wording:

Current:

> growing as an understory palm beneath taller canopy trees in humid conditions with consistent moisture and dappled light.

Maybe:

> **It grows beneath taller rainforest trees, where the light is filtered and the ground stays moist.**

Same information, less plant-label language.

### What it does here

This is much better:

> this is one of the quieter oddballs in it.

I like that. It gives the species some personality without overselling it.
